title: Who warned first, and how long before
standfirst: For Lisbon's worst hours on Wednesday, who said what, in what order, and how many hours ahead: IPMA, civil protection, the government, Web Summit. Every time is the issuer's own where the data room has it.

warnings_in_force.about: The official warnings a weather story states first: resolved from IPMA's open data in the data room when the page is built, and read again in the reader's browser.

sections.title: The weather service and civil protection

claims.text: The first signal for the mainland was IPMA's: communiqué no. 1 named the storm on Monday 9 November at 13:17, said orange warnings would follow and did not rule out an upgrade. That is 46.7 hours before Lisbon's red wind warning begins, at 12:00 on Wednesday.
claims.label: fact

supports.field: lead_times[warning=storm named, orange expected, upgrade possible].lead_hours

claims.text: Ten minutes later, at 13:27, IPMA sent a wind warning message for the Lisbon district. Its level is no longer in the feed: it is the message the red warning later replaced.
claims.label: fact

contains: its level is not in the feed any more

claims.text: Civil protection came next: ANEPC's public warning, Aviso 21, on Monday at 20:30, 39.5 hours ahead, before any red warning existed.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: IPMA sent the red wind warning for Lisbon on Tuesday at 07:18:40, for Wednesday 12:00 to 21:00: 28.7 hours ahead.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: The press we could read had it 47 minutes later (Diário de Notícias' live blog, 08:05), and Lusa's piece gave the warning's time as 08:31: about an hour and a quarter after IPMA sent it.
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: Diário de Notícias (live blog); Lusa, as published by AWAY

claims.text: The government followed IPMA by about two hours: the Interior Minister announced the alert situation at ANEPC's press conference, reported from 09:14 to 09:17 on Tuesday; the minute he spoke is not established.
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: the Interior Minister, as reported by Observador's and Diário de Notícias' live blogs

claims.text: The government's own page with the measures is timed 12:10. The alert situation covers Wednesday from 00:00 to 23:59.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: The rain warning came later and then moved. IPMA first made Lisbon's rain red at 16:30 on Tuesday, for 12:00 on Wednesday: 19.5 hours ahead. At 21:23 it moved the start to 09:00, which left 11.6 hours; the orange rain before it was moved to 00:00, 2.6 hours ahead.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: IPMA's own open-data feed ran behind its warnings: the 21:23 change appeared there only between 23:22 and 23:51, at least two hours later.
claims.label: fact

contains: lagged the CAP messages by at least 2 h

claims.text: That move to 09:00 had not been reported in any article title or live-blog entry the media watch could read by 00:15 on Wednesday.
claims.label: hypothesis
claims.confidence: limited by method: matched by title only; four outlets refuse automated reads

claims.text: Web Summit's decision came last. First the government's recommendation to suspend Wednesday, reported at 17:53 on Tuesday, with the decision left to the organisers.
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: the Government, as reported by Jornal de Negócios' live blog (no government page was found)

claims.text: Then the organisers' own page, published at 19:09: "Day 2 (Wednesday, November 11th) will not take place".
claims.label: fact

claims.text: Set in order, with the hours between: IPMA's red wind warning (07:18), the government's alert about two hours after it, the government's recommendation to Web Summit ten and a half hours after it (17:53), the organisers' decision 11 hours 50 minutes after it (19:09).
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: this desk, subtracting the times in the sentences it names

claims.text: The press had the organisers' decision about half an hour after the page went up: ECO at 19:41.
claims.label: evidence

claims.text: Was there an earlier sign? Our meteorologist's hypothesis: the low the US National Hurricane Center followed from 2 November, labelled AL94 on 6 November and dropped on 8 November, was absorbed by the low that became CHARLES. If so, a precursor about nine days ahead: in the analysis's words, "weak signals, not warnings". Its status there: "not established".
claims.label: hypothesis
claims.said_by: incident.meteorologist@web-summit.dinis (analysis; not IPMA's or NHC's words)

supports.expect: the new non-tropical low that absorbed AL94 is, or became part of, CHARLES

not_known.text: The minute the Interior Minister announced the alert situation: 09:14 is the earliest report; the government's page is timed 12:10.
The level of IPMA's first wind message for Lisbon (9 November, 13:27): it left the feed when the red warning replaced it.
The exact minutes between Web Summit's page (19:09:00) and ECO (19:41:31): the timeline says 32 minutes, the media watch's table 33. This story says about half an hour.
When the government told Web Summit: its recommendation is known only from the press (first report 17:53); no government page was found.
Whether these lead times were enough. That is a judgement, not in the data room, and not made here.
Madeira's warnings and what was measured there: a story of its own, to come.
